# Problem 1
```{r import dataset and libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(ggridges)
data("ny_noaa")
```

## Description 
This dataset contains New York temperature, precipitation and snow data collected from 1981 - 2010. There are `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables including `r names(ny_noaa)`, which describe a day's minimum and maximum temperature, inches of precipitation, snow and/or snow depth. However, about 44% of observations are missing data for minimum and maximum temperature. 

```{r data cleaning }

#creating seperate variables for date
ny_noaa  = ny_noaa |>
janitor::clean_names() |>
mutate(
    year  = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day   = day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax), 
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin)
)

#looking at temperature, precipitation, and snowfall for reasonable units

ny_noaa_summary = 
  ny_noaa|>
summarize(
  across(prcp:tmin, 
         list(min = min, max = max, mean = mean, median=median),
         na.rm = TRUE)
  )

#converting variables into reasonable units
ny_noaa = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  mutate( prcp = prcp/10,
          tmin = tmin/10, 
          tmax = tmax/10)

#checking my work 
 ny_noaa_summary = 
  ny_noaa|>
summarize(
  across(prcp:tmin, 
         list(min = min, max = max, mean = mean, median=median),
         na.rm = TRUE)
  )
         

#looking at precipitation specifically
ny_noaa |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = prcp)) + 
  geom_histogram()
#the vast majority of days have no precipitation, but there are some high precipitation days 


ny_noaa  |> 
  filter(prcp >= 1000) # there are 653 observations with over 100mm

ny_noaa |> 
 arrange(desc(prcp)) |>
head()
# there is a record on 1982-08-20 of 2286 mm precipitation, and 1983-04-08 of 2032.5 mm precipitation.  This seems unreasonable. 


#what is the most common value for snowfall
ny_noaa  |>
  count(snow, name = "n_obs")
```

Ensure observations for temperature, precipitation, and snowfall are given in reasonable units. For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? Why?


Response:
Given the summary values of the variables and geography climate of new york, I infer that the variables are initially reported in the following units. 
prcp: 0.1mm (mean= 29.8, max = 22860)
snow fall: mm (mean = 4.98, max = 10160)
snow depth: mm (mean = 37.3, max = 9195)
temperature min: 0.1 Celcius (median = 33)
temperature max: 0.1 Celcius (median = 150)

I have adjusted them to be more interpretable and standardized. 
prcp: mm 
snow fall: mm (no change)
snow depth: mm (no change)
temperature min: Celcius
temperature max: Celcius

There are some unreasonable values, such as highest value of precipitation of 2286mm, and smallest value of snowfall of -13 mm. The tmin min and tmax max is 60 C, which seems unreasonable, inidicating the reporting thermometer was broken, as they were both reported from the same location ID: USR0000NGAN and span of time 08-17-2008 through 09-16-2008. 

The most commonly observed values for snowfall are 0, 3, 5 and 8 

## Plots

Make a two-panel plot showing the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years. Is there any observable / interpretable structure? Any outliers?
For July, it is relatively more stable and less variability than in January, where the ranges are wider. 
For July, the average hovers around 27 C, while in January, it flucuates around 0 C. 
There are outliers. For January, there was a cold day with a mean_tmax of approx -14C around 1982. For July, there is an outlier around 1988 of a mean_tmax of 14C.

# Problem 2
Load, tidy, merge, and otherwise organize the data sets. Your final dataset should include all originally observed variables; exclude participants less than 21 years of age, and those with missing demographic data; and encode data with reasonable variable classes (i.e. not numeric, and using factors with the ordering of tables and plots in mind).


```{r creating datasets}

#importing
accel_df = read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_accel.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() 

covar_df = read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_covar.csv" , na = c("NA", ".", ""), skip =4)|>
janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na()|>
  filter(age >=21) |>
  mutate( #encoding sex and education as factor variable as they are categories
    sex = as.factor(sex), 
    sex = recode(sex, 
                         `1` = "Male", 
                         `2` = "Female"),
    education = as.factor(education),
    education = recode(education, 
                         `1` = "Less than high school", 
                         `2` = "High school equivalent",
                        `3` = "More than high school")
  )

#merging 

nhanes_df = 
  left_join(covar_df, accel_df, by = "seqn")

nhanes_df


```


Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category, and create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category. Comment on these items.

```{r}
nhanes_df |> 
  group_by(education, sex) |> 
janitor::tabyl(education, sex)

nhanes_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, fill = sex)) + 
  geom_boxplot(position = "dodge")+
  geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label = after_stat(count)),position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Sex Among Edcuation Level of Study Participants", x = "Education Level", y = "Number of Participants")

nhanes_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex))+ 
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~education) 

```


The boxplot comparisions of age distribution by sex and education level show that among "less than high school" and "more than high school" groups, age distribution between males and females are relatively similar. "Less than highschool" ranges are higher than "More than high school." 
This is also true for subject counts, as females and males contribute similarly to subject counts, in both "Less than high school" (27 Male , 28 Female) and "More than Highschool" (Male= 56, Fmeale = 59). "More than Highschool" is the education level with the most participants. 


For the "High school equivalent" group, males' interquartile range of age is lower than of females'. In this group, the females' interquartile range of age is the oldest among education levels. Subject count distribution is also nonequivalent by sex, with 35 Males and 23 Females. 

Traditional analyses of accelerometer data focus on the total activity over the day. Using your tidied dataset, aggregate across minutes to create a total activity variable for each participant. Plot these total activities (y-axis) against age (x-axis); your plot should compare men to women and have separate panels for each education level. Include a trend line or a smooth to illustrate differences. Comment on your plot.

```{r}
# creating variable for total activity variable for each participant
nhanes_df =
  nhanes_df |> 
  mutate( 
    total_time = rowSums(across(min1:min1440),na.rm = TRUE) 
    )

# plot total time
nhanes_df |>
 ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_time)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = sex),alpha = .5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) + 
  facet_grid(.~education)

#plot 24-hour activity
nhanes_df_pivot = 
 nhanes_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "min",
    values_to = "mims" ) |>
   separate(min, into = c("mins", "mins_time"), sep = 3) |>
  select (-mins)|>
  mutate ( mins_time = as.numeric(mins_time))

nhanes_df_pivot |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mins_time, y =mims)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = factor(sex)), size = 1, alpha = .5) + # is this needed?
  geom_smooth(aes(color = sex),se = FALSE) + #is it cumulative? 
 labs(
    title = "24-hour activity time courses",
    x = "Minutes",
    y = "MIMS",
    color = "Sex") + 
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(60, 120, 180, 240, 300, 360, 420, 480, 540, 600, 660, 720, 780, 840, 900, 960, 1020, 1080, 1140, 1200, 1260, 1320, 1380, 1440), 
    labels = c("1:00", "2:00", "3:00", "4:00","5:00", "6:00", "7:00", "8:00","9:00","10:00", "11:00", "12:00",
               "13:00", "14:00", "15:00", "16:00","17:00", "18:00", "19:00", "20:00","21:00","22:00", "23:00", "24:00"))+facet_wrap(~education, ncol = 1)

# for every individual or sum/average of education level


```

  
Between males and female, there does not appear to be a distinct trend, They are scattered throughout the plots. Less the highschool has the most distinct sharpest downward trend, where total activity time decreases with age. High school equivalent education level has a trend spoke around age 40, and then total activity decreases with age. Among more than highschool, there is a platued trend around 13000 total activity time until 50, where total activity time decreases with age.

# Problem 3 
```{r importing data}

citijan2020_df = read_csv(file = "./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2020, month = "Jan")

citijuly2020_df = read_csv(file = "./data/July 2020 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2020, month = "Jul")


citijan2024_df = read_csv(file = "./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2024, month = "Jan")

citijuly2024_df = read_csv(file = "./data/July 2024 Citi.csv", 
                      na = c("NA", ".", ""))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |> 
          mutate(year = 2024, month ="Jul")

citi_df = 
  bind_rows(citijan2020_df,citijuly2020_df, citijan2024_df, citijuly2024_df) |>
  janitor::clean_names()
```

There were relatively few electric Citi Bikes in 2020, but many more are available now. For data in 2024, make a figure that shows the impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration. Comment on your results.

# individually? 

```{r citi2024}
citi_2024_df = 
citi_df |> 
filter(year == 2024) 

#month
month_density = 
citi_2024_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, fill = month)) + 
   geom_density(alpha = .4, adjust = .5, color = "blue")+
  labs(
    title = " Distribution of Ride Duration between Jan and July 2024",
    x = "Ride Duration in Minutes")

#membership 
membership_density= 
citi_2024_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, fill = member_casual)) + 
   geom_density(alpha = .4, adjust = .5, color = "blue")+
  labs(
    title = " Distribution of Ride Duration between Membership Status",
    x = "Ride Duration in Minutes")


#bike type
bike_density=
citi_2024_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = duration, fill = rideable_type)) + 
   geom_density(alpha = .4, adjust = .5, color = "blue")+
  labs(
    title = " Distribution of Ride Duration by Bike Type",
    x = "Ride Duration in Minutes")

(month_density/membership_density/bike_density)


```


The density plot of the Distribution of Ride Duration between Jan and July 2024, shows that riders in January rode for shorter durations compared to July. Given the weather differences between January (with snow) and July, this makes sense. 

The density plot of the Distribution of Ride Duration between Membership Status shows that more members rode shorter durations, while casual riders had more longer rides. 

The density plot of Distribution of Ride Duration by Bike Type shows that ride duration of classic and electric bikes are very similar, with electric bikes very slighly more longer rides.
